sites.name: Leicester
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw, and the start of the Soar variant. Æthelflæd of Mercia took it back from the Danes in 918.

sites.name: Heath Wood, Ingleby
sites.text: The only known Viking cremation cemetery in Britain: around 60 barrows in the wood above the Trent, on the Repton extension.

sites.name: Repton
sites.text: At the end of the Repton extension, up the Trent from Derby. The Great Heathen Army wintered here in 873–874 and drove out the Mercian king; a Viking camp and burials have been excavated by the church.

sites.name: Derby
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs. Its name is Old Norse, Djúrabý, "deer farm". Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, took it back from the Danes in 917.

sites.name: Nottingham
sites.text: Another of the Five Boroughs. The Great Heathen Army wintered here in 867–868.

sites.name: Stow Minster
sites.text: Off the route, 5 km from Torksey. A great Anglo-Saxon minster with the earliest known carving of a Viking ship in England scratched into a pillar.

sites.name: Torksey
sites.text: The Great Army's winter camp of 872–873, where the Fossdyke meets the Trent. Excavation and metal-detecting have found thousands of finds: hack silver, weights and lead gaming pieces.

sites.name: Fossdyke
sites.text: A canal joining the Trent at Torksey to the Witham at Lincoln, probably Roman and still navigable.

sites.name: Gainsborough
sites.text: On the Trent north of Torksey. Sweyn Forkbeard, king of Denmark, made it his base when he conquered England in 1013 and died there in 1014.

sites.name: Lincoln
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs, with a busy Viking-age mint. Lincoln was the chief town of Lindsey, the old kingdom that the Danes divided into three ridings, from the Old Norse þriðjungr, a third: the Lindsey Ridings take their name from them. The Lindsey Ridings leaves north-east for Grimsby and the Humber coast.

sites.name: Stamford
sites.text: The fifth of the Five Boroughs, on the Welland, with a Danish fortified borough north of the river. The coast route turns down the Welland here.

sites.name: Crowland
sites.text: Crowland Abbey stands in the Fens by the Welland. Later medieval chronicles claimed the Danes burned it in 870, though that account is now thought unreliable.

sites.name: Skegness
sites.text: Its name is Old Norse: Skeggi's ness, the headland of a man called Skeggi.

sites.name: Lincolnshire Wolds
sites.text: Tealby, Normanby, Grimsby and dozens more: Lincolnshire has more Old Norse -by place names than any other English county, many of them strung along these chalk hills. The route runs close to the Viking Way footpath from here to Barton.

sites.name: Barton-upon-Humber
sites.text: The old ferry town on the south bank of the Humber. St Peter's Church has an Anglo-Saxon tower from around the end of the 10th century.

sites.name: Grimsby
sites.text: On the Humber coast: by tradition named after Grim, a Danish fisherman, with the Old Norse -by for farm or village. The Lindsey Ridings reaches the sea here.

sites.name: Humber
sites.text: The estuary the Great Army crossed on its way to York in 866. The Lindsey Ridings crosses it on the Humber Bridge.

sites.name: Leeds
sites.text: Leeds Minster keeps a 10th-century Anglo-Scandinavian stone cross carved with Weland the Smith, a hero of Norse legend. Start of the Aire variant.

sites.name: Castleford
sites.text: In 948 the army of Viking York under Eric Bloodaxe caught King Eadred's rearguard here and slaughtered it, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records.

sites.name: Selby
sites.text: A name of Old Norse origin, probably "willow farm", like many -by places along the Way.

sites.name: Riccall
sites.text: Harald Hardrada's fleet came up the Ouse and landed here in September 1066, the last great Viking invasion of England.

sites.name: Fulford
sites.text: Harald Hardrada beat the northern earls here on 20 September 1066, five days before his defeat at Stamford Bridge.

sites.name: Stamford Bridge
sites.text: At the end of the Stamford Bridge extension, east of York. Harold Godwinson defeated and killed Harald Hardrada here on 25 September 1066, the end of the Viking Age in England.

sites.name: York
sites.text: Jorvik. The Great Heathen Army took it on 1 November 866, and it was the capital of a Viking kingdom until Eric Bloodaxe was driven out in 954.
